beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, just a section title

beats.trigger: The hard part is not access; it is absorption.
beats.got: Rolling out an agent is the easy bit and getting people to use it is the real problem. I half knew that but hadn't put it in one line.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: nothing new. I have three of those from our own Confluence.

beats.trigger: **Interview** for your teammate's job-to-be-done using the agentic Jobs-to-be-Done pattern
beats.got: nothing new, it's a list of verbs. The JTBD name-dropping reads like consultant talk.

beats.trigger: Two questions to warm up: who's the one person who came to mind just now?
beats.got: I'd already have thought of the sales team. The rest is setup.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the colleague's job, not from my agent. Fair, but it is the standard product-discovery line.

beats.trigger: If the agent ranges too wide, interrupt with *"tell me what you've found so far, narrow to the files that bear on this teammate, then continue."*
beats.got: The agent reads my files and writes a JTBD file. The tip about interrupting an agent that goes too wide or too shallow is the only new bit. I'd skip the reading step and let it run.

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is a vendor pitch and is NOT on the list.
beats.got: There are four sharing shapes: context, skill, push output, pull interface. That sorts out what I'd been mashing together.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a hand-off line

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new, the exercise intro

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Pick the one obstacle that makes the others hard, not the first technical limit I see. I'd normally go straight to the technical one.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: My technical plans always look done while the people side is blank. That describes what I build.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: nothing new, it's a hand-off line

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until they are tested. Obvious, but fine.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: I should test whether they'd switch before I build. I'd have built it first.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: Imagine the failure first and write three stories. It is a failure mode I hadn't tried on my own rollouts. It ends in one named person and one question, which is concrete.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Picking by what fits our stack is shopping. Picking by outcome is design.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of it.
beats.got: nothing new, a lecture intro

beats.trigger: Speed and quality alone means it went shallow.
beats.got: Look for a third outcome like a removed dependency or an anxiety gone. This repeats the exercise.

beats.trigger: They run it, get a generic answer, and quietly stop.
beats.got: The agent file is just the shell. The real work is in my curated memory and corrections. Engineers on my team have done exactly that: copied my setup and quietly dropped it.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily, but someone has to answer for the agent. A shared agent is three parts of four.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute.
beats.got: nothing new, it's the big idea again in longer form

beats.trigger: Michael Polanyi, a philosopher of science, had the line for it: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: People pick up what resembles what they already do. The philosopher quote is decoration for me.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: The interface is the first piece that involves another person. Okay.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The rival is their spreadsheet or gut call, so it has to land where they already look and work the first time. Nobody asked sales for my weekend build, and this says why that matters.

beats.trigger: You can hand over four things, and none of them is what you learned.
beats.got: They decide whether to adopt, not me. It's a bit poetic.

beats.trigger: A missing name is a finding: it marks the part of this that is not built yet
beats.got: An empty name field is the result, not a gap in the exercise. I'd have filled it with a guess.

beats.trigger: Notice what this prompt insists on: name the path, overwrite in place, quote the before-and-after for every claim.
beats.got: Another review of the artifact by the agent. It's ceremony. I'd skip it, and I likely would have skipped the before-and-after check.

beats.trigger: Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Four ways to share: the context, a skill, the output (push), an interface (pull). Never the whole agent.
beats.got: A recap I didn't need.

beats.trigger: Come to Module 8 without one tested assumption or named person and you'll be reconstructing the contact
beats.got: I need to talk to one real person before the next module. A fair assignment.

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Don't build for the sales team first. Start from one person's job and their current way of doing it, and ask what would have to be true for them to switch.
You can't share an agent as one thing. Context, boundary and checks copy easily, but someone still has to answer for it, and that's the part nobody has named.
An empty name in the people plan means the plan isn't done, however clean the technical plan looks.

monday.move: Ask one sales person how they prepare for a customer call today, before I build or share anything. Then put the unassigned owner question on my own plan.
monday.who: One sales lead I already know, plus whoever would maintain it. I don't know yet who that is.
monday.when: Tuesday, 30 minutes, if I remember. Probably not Monday.
monday.stop_condition: If they say they're fine with what they have, I drop the sales build.
monday.blocker: Nobody outside engineering has asked for it, and I haven't found anyone to own it. I'd rather just build it.

misconception.why: The module is about adoption, not about checking output. I skipped the review and debrief steps and lost nothing. The 'competing with their spreadsheet' beat made me doubt the sales build, but that is a doubt about demand, not about whether good output needs checking.

one_line: Good for a leader who builds first and asks later, and the 'accountability doesn't copy' idea is worth the price. Half of it is the same point repeated, and the debrief is ceremony.
